title: Which open hydraulic circuit gets a small excavator closest to stock energy use for the least money?
lede: research programme: which buildable hydraulic circuit gets a small excavator closest to stock energy use; on a measured 6 t load-sensing wheel loader (Zenodo, CC BY) the measured LS margin is 24.9 bar, the model's LS rung matches measured pump energy to 2.3%, and an open-centre pump on the same motion needs at least 1.37 times the energy for any bypass law (1.54 times and 14.7% more fuel at a 10 bar spool drop, with the motion threshold measured from the data); its break-even LS margin (87 bar against 20 to 30 on synthetic cycles) splits exactly into (pump volume / demand volume − 1) times the pressure the surplus flow is pushed at (99.5 bar on the loader, 34 bar under its 134 bar working pressure) plus idle bleed; a smaller fixed pump reaches the measured margin only at about 28.5 cc and 39% more cycle time; priced in the record's own fuel, open-centre burns 11.5% more fuel per unit of work than load-sensing at its best pump (53.5 cc) and no pump size breaks even; on ten measured truck-loading recordings of a large excavator (Hugging Face, CC BY-NC-SA) the highest live hydraulic pressure while the arm moves is a median 174 bar, 5.3 times the force model's 33 bar, which lifts the synthetic break-even margin from about 11 to 24 to 59 bar; on a 7.5 t class excavator's measured joint motion a fixed pump delivers 2.4 times the oil the work uses, and a half-size fixed pump (108 L/min) matches load-sensing pump energy for 11% more cycle time, against 39% on the loader; earlier milestones are model sweeps with sourced margins and valve curves
summary: An open research programme on which hydraulic circuit a small shop can build from catalogue parts to get a 1.5 to 3 t excavator closest to stock energy use, and at what parts cost. Milestone 1 is a stdlib model of pump-shaft energy for three circuits (fixed-displacement open-centre, load-sensing, ideal independent metering; analytic single-actuator check, 6 tests) and a 2,916-case grid on one four-phase cycle: load-sensing uses a median 47% of open-centre shaft energy (22 to 81%), saving more as flow demand falls (31%, 47%, 63% of open-centre at 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0 of full flow), and metering uses a median 80% of load-sensing, 88% with equal actuator pressures and 74% at 1.5 times the reference spread. The ordering holds in every case but only because each rung removes a loss term, so it is a code check rather than a finding. The cycle, pressures, flows and margins are illustrative values written from memory and swept, not sourced; there are no dynamics, leakage, line losses, energy recovery or parts costs; the DOI registry was unreachable so references were checked by web search, not cite_check. Milestone 2a repeats the comparison on 20,000 random cycles inside a machine envelope (pump 45 L/min, 20 to 180 bar, taken from an unopened search summary of one mini-excavator listing): load-sensing uses a median 44% of open-centre energy, metering 72% of load-sensing (87% at equal actuator pressures), and H3 fails per case in about a third of equal-pressure cycles. The cycles are random, not measured. Preliminary; arithmetic only, nothing run on a machine. Milestone 5n (2026-11-11) adds the first measured machine: a public 440 s trace of a 6 t load-sensing wheel loader loading gravel (Linjama et al., Zenodo 10639199, CC BY 4.0) with pump and cylinder pressures, flows and ECU fuel rate. The measured load-sensing margin is a median 24.9 bar (standby 30.8 bar); the model's constant-margin load-sensing rung reproduces measured pump hydraulic energy to 2.3% (per-cycle 95% bootstrap 1.3 to 3.4%); actuators receive 73% of pump hydraulic energy. A counterfactual open-centre pump on the same motion would use 1.46 times the hydraulic energy (sweep 1.24 to 1.79) and add 12.3% to machine fuel (6.2 to 21.7%), refuting two of four registered predictions; the figure depends most on a small-flow threshold for the open-centre bypass chosen after a first, buggy run. A wheel loader, not an excavator; valve drops swept, not sourced. Milestone 5o measures that threshold instead: the flow noise floor in windows where the piston does not move is 0.80 L/min (lift) and 1.76 L/min (tilt); with it, open-centre needs 1.54 times the load-sensing pump hydraulic energy (per-cycle 95% bootstrap 1.46 to 1.63) and adds 14.7% fuel at a 10 bar spool drop, and a floor valid for any bypass closing law (spool drop 0) is 1.37 to 1.43 times. A motion rule from piston position alone gives 1.51. All four registered predictions held. With the least drop any Danfoss PVG 32 spool can have fully open (milestone 5r), the ratio is 1.42 (11.3% more fuel): on this machine the open-centre penalty comes from the fixed pump, not the spool. The lift flow exceeds the largest PVG 32 spool's rating in 11% of moving samples, where that floor is extrapolated. Milestone 5t evaluates the closed-form break-even margin on this record: load-sensing would match the best open-centre counterfactual only at an 87 bar margin (per Y-cycle 59 to 143 bar, median 81), against 20 to 30 bar on the synthetic excavator cycles, so the measured 24.9 bar margin leaves large headroom; about 90% of it is surplus flow from a fixed pump whose mean flow is 1.78 times the mean demand. The counterfactual keeps the loader's own pump size. Milestone 5u splits that margin exactly: m* = β[(r−1)p + covariance + r·d] + idle, where r is the fixed pump's volume over the volume the work needs while moving and p the working pressure. On the synthetic cycles r = 1.43 and p only 33 bar, so the surplus term is 12 bar and idle bleed adds 8; a two-number rule (r−1)p reads 31% low, and with idle put back it is within 6%. The loader's r of 1.78 and an implied working pressure near 100 bar (to be checked when the data host is reachable) explain its fourfold higher break-even. Milestone 5v checked that on the loader: its demand-weighted working pressure is 134 bar, and the exact form needs the pressure the surplus flow is pushed at, 99.5 bar; using the working pressure overstates the break-even by about 30%. Milestone 5w lets the open-centre counterfactual pick a smaller fixed pump, slowing the actuators where demand exceeds it: the break-even falls to the measured 24.9 bar margin only at about 28.5 cc (45% of the loader's 63 cc), where open-centre needs 1.39 times load-sensing's cycle time (per Y-cycle 1.27 to 1.54); every pump of 40 cc or more still loses on energy. 5x prices that time in the record's own ECU fuel: with the extra time charged at the rest of the machine's measured 5.15 L/h and the record's Willans slope (0.233 L/kWh), open-centre burns 11.5% more fuel per unit of work than load-sensing at its best fixed pump (53.5 cc), 13.0% at 63 cc and 26% at the 28.5 cc energy-parity pump; no size from 25 to 63 cc, no pump efficiency from 0.75 to 0.95 and none of the 18 Y-cycles breaks even (6.2 to 6.8% even if the extra time burned only near-idle fuel). The extra time is charged at a constant measured rate, not simulated, and the record carries no payload. On a measured excavator (5y, 5z; Hugging Face fuxi-robot/excavator-motion, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, derived statistics only), a 49 t class machine works at a median 174 bar while moving, 5.3 times the force model, and the joint motion of a 7.5 t class machine, turned into cylinder flow with published cylinder sizes, gives a pump-to-demand volume ratio of 2.38 for a fixed pump sized at the p99 demand (1.95 to 3.08 across lever, sign and swing assumptions; loader 1.79, synthetic 1.43), so the break-even load-sensing margin is 70 to 140 bar, several times any margin sold. Flow and pressure come from different machines and no excavator fuel record exists yet.
